But she looks at Wren's set face and decides the girl will not be easy until the slab is shut, so they will go down to Stonebridge when you and the crew are back, around noon tomorrow. The oil sloshes in its crocks. A small shape is trying to hide behind the cart wheel. It is not hiding well.

input.description: Seal the slab and stair in the Ford Chapel (roofless chapel at the ford, an hour south of the Millstone Inn), a mound of the Sleepers' Chain, with capstone, clay and oil before it opens. Party at first light on Day 9: Brannoc, Corwin Reed, Osric, Tobias (Maud's cousin, cart and mule), the apprentice Fenn, with a dozen village flasks of oil plus Brannoc's. Wren is to carry a lamp but stay back. Maud and Wren will wait to go to Stonebridge until it is sealed.
relationships: part of the Sleepers' Chain, see [[Ruined chapel at the ford]]

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Ford Chapel sealing party; added 2 relationships to Ford Chapel sealing party

Maud answers your question first, with a sniff. She and Wren will not go to Stonebridge until the slab is shut. "It's on the road. I'm not walking my girl past a hole in the ground I've heard about." She says it as if it were her own idea, and Wren, who has been hearing every word, pretends not to be pleased.

You spend the evening as you said you would. Ilsa has her cheeks full and Tessa asleep and easy. You count a slow sixty at the window and the baby's breath comes quiet and even. Osric's arm is closing, and Wren's linen is clean. The villagers eat well and early, and Tobias grumbles about the hour but stacks the capstone, ropes and wedges in the cart. Wren sweeps the chapel floor around your pallet until she is sent home again. Sleep comes quick, and the long rest takes you.

You wake at ten to five on Day 9 in the cold, dark chapel, with all your hit points and three 1st-level slots, and Channel Divinity ready. Outside, the cart is waiting with the mule snorting in the cold. Corwin has lit the lantern, Osric is yawning, Tobias is checking the rope, and Fenn clutches a crowbar as if he might break it. There's a heap of oil flasks, your forty-five and the village's dozen. Wren is on the step with a shuttered lamp, looking fierce.

You can change your prepared list now. Your plan is the capstone and clay, the oil, and the cart-mule to drag the slab home, with everyone ready to pull back to the cart at the first sign of trouble. The Ford Chapel is two hours south. It's about ten to five on Day 9, and you're 100 XP short of level 3.

Maud and Wren will wait until the slab is sealed. That's my ruling, and Maud's own choice. She isn't taking a twelve-year-old down a road past an open barrow, and she says so flatly. They'll go to Stonebridge the day after, with the weather fair and the road safe.

The evening is quiet. You count Tessa's breaths in Ilsa's window, a slow sixty, easy and even. Osric's arm is closing clean under Wren's linen. Corwin and Hale feed you at their table, and Hale watches you eat like a woman checking a loaf. Tobias oils the cart axle. Corwin sharpens the crowbar. Nobody says much, and nobody sleeps badly. Wren sweeps the chapel one last time and goes home to bed under protest.

entries.text: notebook: updated Marta Quill

You unbar the door, mace in your left hand, shield on your arm, and step into the doorway with the lantern opened a hand's breadth. You call to her gently, and she lifts her head and stumbles the last twenty paces toward your voice. You keep your eyes on her the whole way, and the Drowned Stair is not far from your mind.

You answer your own question first. In the lantern-light she throws a shadow long and clear behind her on the causeway. There is no frost on her lips and no gray finger-mark on her. She is a living woman, and she walks like one who is dying slowly of something ordinary.

Medicine (16): she is thirty or so, thin, wrapped in a reed-cutter's wool cloak. Her skin burns to the touch, and the shaking in her hands is a chill, not a fear. The whites of her eyes have a yellow tinge, her head aches so she can barely lift it, and when you press under her ribs she gasps. That is the marsh-fever, the one the carters spoke of. She is two days into it. It is dangerous but not yet at its worst, and a fever of this kind can kill in a week without care. It's a disease, which Lesser Restoration could end.

She says her name is Marta Quill, of Reedholm, and she was walking to Stonebridge for a healer for her small son Dab, who is sick with the same. She sags against your arm and says, in a cracked voice, "Sedge is my sister's boy. They said the lights came when the reed-cutters cut the stand by the drowned barrow. Everyone who cut there is down. Everyone." Then she coughs for a long time.

You take her weight and help her to the bench by the fire. It's twenty-six minutes past ten on Day 11. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, and a pouch of willow-bark. The hut is warm. Marta has a burning brow and a dying lantern, and she looks at you as if you're the end of a very long road.

input.add_to_description: Day 11 ~10:30 PM: Brannoc examined her at the hut door (Medicine 16, Insight 17): living, casts a shadow, fever-flushed, lips cracked and dry, not frost-burned. Marsh-fever: hot dry skin, shivering, wet cough, yellowish eyes. Honest and frightened. Her son Dab (age 6) is sick at Reedholm with his aunt.

entries.text: notebook: updated Marta Quill

You unbar the door and step into the doorway with the hooded lantern opened a hand's width, shield on your arm and mace in the other hand. You call to her as you planned. She flinches at the voice and then stumbles toward you.

Your questions first. Yes, she casts a shadow. It slides long and wavering across the road behind her in the lantern's last light. Her lips are cracked and dry, flushed with fever, with no frost-burn and no gray marks on her hands or throat.

Medicine (16): this is a living woman with a fever. Her skin is hot and dry, her eyes have a faint yellow cast, and she shivers hard in bursts. There is a wet, tearing cough. The sweat on her has an ugly sweetish smell, like standing marsh-water. Her pulse is fast and thin. It is not the lung-fever Piper had, but something that settles in the blood and the belly, the marsh-fever the carters named. Insight (17): she is frightened and honest. She is exactly what she seems.

You get her to the fire and into your blanket, and you hold a cup of water with a pinch of the willow-bark to her lips. She sips and sags. Her name is Marta Quill, a reed-cutter's wife from Reedholm, and she has been walking two days to reach Stonebridge for a healer for her son. Dab is six and sick as she is, and he's with his aunt. She talks in bursts, in between shaking fits. The Wick-fires started when the cutters went into the reeds near the drowned barrow, she says, to cut the thick old reeds on the mound for the winter thatch. Every one who cut there is sick. Her nephew Sedge was one. He took the eels to market because the elders would not let anyone else go.

She won't sleep until you promise that someone will see Dab. She stares at you with fever-bright eyes, and her grip on your wrist is hot and strong.

It's twenty-five to eleven on Day 11. You have four 1st-level slots and two 2nd-level slots, Lesser Restoration, Channel Divinity, and willow-bark. The disease is a true one, and Lesser Restoration would end it. Reedholm is a day and a half on, and she'd never make it back on her own.

What does Brannoc do?

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 3: 15 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

I unbar the door, keeping my mace in my left hand and my shield on my arm, and step into the doorway with the hooded lantern opened a little. "Over here, goodwife, the door's open. I'm Brannoc, a healer. Come to the fire and sit, and don't try to talk yet."

Before she crosses the threshold I'll look her over: her lips and eyes for blue or yellow, her hands, and whether she walks like someone sick or something else, since I'm wary after the Drowned Stair. DM: does she cast a shadow and do her lips show any frost-burn like the gray marks on Tobin's ankle?

input.add_to_description: Day 11 10:20 PM: Living, casts a shadow, no frost-burn. Real marsh-fever. Brannoc's Medicine read (10) was inconclusive about how advanced it is or whether she is contagious.

entries.text: notebook: updated Marta Quill

You unbar the door and step into the doorway with the mace low in your left hand, your shield on your arm, and the hooded lantern opened a little. You call out as you planned. The bent shape lifts its head at your voice and nearly falls.

You look her over as she comes into the light, and you answer your own caution plainly. She casts a shadow, a thin long one thrown by the dying lantern in her hand. Her lips are cracked and dry and flushed, with no blue and no gray on them, and no frost-burn anywhere that you can see. Her breath steams in the cold like anyone's. She is a living woman, thirty or so, in a reed-cutter's patched wool, with mud to her thighs. Her cheeks are high with fever and her eyes are too bright. She's shivering hard, even as sweat runs down her face.

Medicine (10): beyond that, you can't read her well. The fever is real and she is badly spent. You can't tell how far along it is, whether she might mend with rest, or whether it is the kind that spreads from person to person. She might even be worse than she looks.

She reaches the threshold, grips the door-frame, and says in a cracked whisper, "Marta. Marta Quill. From Reedholm. I was going to Stonebridge. My boy... Dab..." Then her knees go, and you catch her under the arms before she hits the floor. She weighs almost nothing.

It's eighteen past ten on Day 11. She is in your arms, fever-hot, breathing fast. You have four 1st-level slots, two 2nd-level slots, Channel Divinity, willow-bark, a jar of honey, and a fire.
